solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: County town with no stone supply (6)

indicatorNotes.with no: the county town is taken without the stone, so ST is removed

blocks.note: Stafford, the county town of Staffordshire
st = stone, the British unit of weight, removed from the front

annotation.surface: A market town has run out of building stone.
annotation.walkthrough: A county town is the administrative centre of an English county. "Supply" is a verb here: to afford comfort is to supply it.
annotation.definitionFit: To afford something, as in affording shelter, is to provide or supply it.

entries.clue: Tyrant’s car, a Tesla, carrying the king (8)

indicatorNotes.carrying: the car and the Tesla carry the king along between them

blocks.note: T is the symbol for the tesla, the SI unit of magnetic flux density

annotation.surface: A despot is driven about in an electric car with the monarch aboard.
annotation.walkthrough: Tesla looks like the car brand, but here it is the physicist's unit, abbreviated T. CR, for Carolus Rex, is a crossword stand-in for the king.
annotation.definitionFit: An autocrat rules with absolute power, which is what a tyrant does.

entries.clue: Kindle addict (3)

blocks.note: the verb: to kindle a fire by blowing air at it

annotation.surface: Someone hooked on their Kindle e-reader.
annotation.walkthrough: Kindle is capitalised to look like the Amazon e-reader; it is really the verb, as in fanning a fire.
annotation.definitionFit: You fan a fire to kindle it, and a fan is someone addicted to a hobby or star.

entries.clue: Noise here voiced by a cockney crook (9)

indicatorNotes.voiced by a cockney: a cockney drops the H, so HERE is said 'ERE

blocks.note: HERE without its H, written to sound the same

annotation.surface: A London villain makes a din right here.
annotation.walkthrough: Cockneys are Londoners whose accent famously drops the H. A racketeer runs a racket, a criminal scheme, so the noise word also hints at the crook.
annotation.definitionFit: A racketeer makes money from dishonest or illegal schemes, so is a crook.

entries.clue: Suckers importing small brown horses (8)

indicatorNotes.importing: the suckers bring the small brown inside them

blocks.note: s = small, as in clothing sizes

annotation.surface: Gullible buyers are shipping in little brown ponies.
annotation.walkthrough: Mugs is British slang for people easily fooled. "Small brown" reads as describing the horses, but it is wordplay tucked inside the suckers.
annotation.definitionFit: Mustangs are the free-roaming horses of the American West.

entries.clue: Greek character leading lions around (7)

indicatorNotes.around: the letters of LIONS are turned around into a new order

blocks.note: up = ahead, leading, as in two goals up

annotation.surface: A figure from Greek myth is heading a pride of lions.
annotation.walkthrough: "Character" means a letter of the alphabet, not a person in a story. Being up in a match means leading it.
annotation.definitionFit: Upsilon is the twentieth letter of the Greek alphabet.

entries.clue: Unknown vessel capsized smuggling a precious mineral (5)

indicatorNotes.capsized: an upturned vessel, in a down clue, reads from the bottom up
indicatorNotes.smuggling: the reversed letters carry A hidden inside them

blocks.note: z = an unknown quantity in algebra

annotation.surface: A mystery boat overturns while running a gemstone past customs.
annotation.walkthrough: Vessel suggests a ship, which fits capsized, but it is a pot. Z and POT together are turned round to give TOPZ, and A goes inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Topaz is a silicate mineral prized as a gemstone.

entries.clue: Zero benefit without country sacking leader occasionally (3,3,5)

indicatorNotes.without: an old sense of without: outside, so NO GAIN wraps round the country
indicatorNotes.sacking leader: the country loses its first letter

blocks.note: RWANDA without its first letter R

annotation.surface: A country gains nothing once it fires its head of state.
annotation.walkthrough: "Without" reads as "lacking" but has its old sense of outside, so zero-benefit wraps round the beheaded country.
annotation.definitionFit: Now and again means from time to time, or occasionally.

entries.clue: String underwear ignored in bistros (6)

indicatorNotes.ignored in: the underwear inside the bistros is left out

blocks.note: bras = underwear, removed from the front

annotation.surface: Nobody in the café notices someone wearing a string.
annotation.walkthrough: String sits right next to underwear to suggest a G-string; it means a sequence, as in a string of wins.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a run of things one after another, as in a string of wins.

entries.clue: Briefly tramp and toff rub shoulders (6)

indicatorNotes.Briefly: the word for tramp is cut short by its last letter

blocks.note: HOBO, a tramp, minus its last O
nob = a toff, an upper-class person

annotation.surface: A vagrant and an aristocrat mingle for a moment.
annotation.walkthrough: Toff and nob are both British slang for someone posh. The surface is itself a picture of hobnobbing across classes.
annotation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially, especially with people of higher status: to rub shoulders.

entries.clue: Firm, after tax returns bill, promises to pay (9)

indicatorNotes.returns: the word for after tax goes back the other way

blocks.note: net pay is what is left after tax
IOUs are written promises to pay

annotation.surface: A company, having got its tax back, issues IOUs.
annotation.walkthrough: Firm looks like a business, a picture the tax and bills keep up; it is an adjective. "Tax returns" suggests paperwork, but the break is after "after tax".
annotation.definitionFit: Tenacious means holding firm and not letting go.

entries.clue: Maths exponent’s faculty (5)

blocks.note: an ability of mind or body, like speech or sight

annotation.surface: A mathematician's university department.
annotation.walkthrough: Exponent reads as a person who champions maths, and faculty as a university department; both are cleaner senses.
annotation.definitionFit: An exponent is a power in maths, and a mental faculty is one of your powers.

entries.clue: Immaculate hosts greeting South American chap (7)

indicatorNotes.hosts: the word for immaculate has the greeting as a guest inside

annotation.surface: A spotless host welcomes a visitor from South America.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hosts" reads as someone welcoming a guest; here it means the greeting sits inside the word for immaculate.
annotation.definitionFit: A Chilean is a man from Chile, in South America.

entries.clue: Insecure duo split up eventually (2,3,6)

indicatorNotes.split up: the letters of INSECURE DUO are broken apart and reset

annotation.surface: An anxious couple finally break up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a relationship that was always going to end, and "split up" is what it does to the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: In due course means at the proper time, later on: eventually.

entries.clue: Four equal sides joined the French, including Australia and England (7)

indicatorNotes.including: the French word LE holds the two countries between its letters

annotation.surface: France teams up with Australia and England to form a four-sided alliance.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like four nations forming a bloc; the first four words are a geometry description.
annotation.definitionFit: A lozenge is a diamond shape: four equal sides joined, with two acute and two obtuse angles.

entries.clue: Wannabe warlord running for PM (6,5,3)

indicatorNotes.running: the letters are set running into a new shape

annotation.surface: An aspiring strongman stands for Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: Andrew Bonar Law was the Conservative who served as British Prime Minister in 1922–23. "Running for" reads as standing for election, but running is the anagram signal and "for" the link.
annotation.definitionFit: Bonar Law was a British prime minister, a PM.

entries.clue: Check railroad for stress (9)

blocks.note: to rein in is to check
to railroad is to force something through

annotation.surface: An inspector examines train tracks for strain.
annotation.walkthrough: Railroad is the verb, pushing something through against resistance, and stress is also a verb, meaning to emphasise.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of emphasis: repeating an argument to strengthen it both stresses and reinforces it.

entries.clue: Get together and walk around Sussex periodically (8)

indicatorNotes.around: the walk goes round the letters from Sussex
indicatorNotes.periodically: only every other letter of Sussex is used

blocks.note: to amble is to walk slowly
S-u-S-s-E-x: first, third and fifth letters

annotation.surface: Friends meet up for a ramble in the Sussex countryside every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: Sussex is a county in southern England. "Periodically" looks like part of the walking plan, but it only picks letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a crowd gathering in a hall is both getting together and assembling.

entries.clue: Three COP claims about fossil fuels (14)

annotation.definitionNote: petrochemicals are made from fossil fuels rather than being fuels themselves; the setter stretches the sense
annotation.surface: Three pledges made at a UN climate summit on coal, oil and gas.
annotation.walkthrough: COP is the UN climate conference, which is why fossil fuels are the talk. "Three" is not a number; its letters are fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum and natural gas, the fossil fuels.

entries.clue: Mixture for freezing blubber, gone wrong (7)

indicatorNotes.wrong: GONE is put wrong, into a different order

blocks.note: to blubber is to cry noisily

annotation.surface: A recipe to preserve whale fat has failed.
annotation.walkthrough: Next to freezing, blubber suggests whale fat; it is the verb for sobbing.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryogen is a freezing mixture or refrigerant used to produce very low temperatures.

entries.clue: One gets excited about oneself primarily (6)

annotation.definition: One gets excited about oneself primarily

indicatorNotes.about: the letters go round the O
indicatorNotes.primarily: only the first letter of oneself is used

annotation.surface: Someone who gets worked up only about themselves.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: an egoist is exactly someone whose excitement is about themselves.
annotation.definitionFit: An egoist is self-centred, so gets excited chiefly about himself or herself.

entries.clue: Bill mostly bowled quickly for example (6)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word is used, losing its last letter

blocks.note: ADVERT, a bill or poster, minus its T

annotation.surface: A cricketer named Bill was mostly bowled out fast.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a batsman's name and quickly like the speed of the ball. In the definition, "quickly" is the example word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the -ly word modifies a verb, which puts it in that part of speech.

entries.clue: Visits doctor before having internal operations (5,2)

indicatorNotes.having internal: DR BY has the operations placed inside

blocks.note: by = before, as in by noon

annotation.surface: A patient sees the GP before undergoing internal surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: "Before" gives BY, as in by noon. "Internal operations" reads as surgery on the inside, but internal tells you where the ops go.
annotation.definitionFit: To drop by is to pay a casual visit, so drops by means visits.

entries.clue: Southern mountain state (5)

annotation.surface: A mountainous state in the South.
annotation.walkthrough: State reads as a region, like a US state, but it is the verb meaning to say.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to put something into words out loud.

entries.clue: Old barrier’s secured following crime (7)

blocks.note: f = following, as in page references

annotation.surface: An ancient fence has been fixed in place after a break-in.
annotation.walkthrough: F for following is the abbreviation used in page references like pp 12f. The barrier sits last, having taken the F on in front of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any breach of the law, from speeding to murder.

entries.clue: Strange European lake (5)

blocks.note: Lake Erie, one of the Great Lakes

annotation.surface: An odd lake somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: Erie is the crossword's favourite lake, one of North America's Great Lakes, so it is anything but European.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the word adds a note of the uncanny, strange in a way that unsettles.

entries.clue: Fancy bar with G&T — and soup (9)

annotation.definition: Fancy bar with G&T — and soup

indicatorNotes.Fancy: the letters are dressed up into a fancier order

blocks.note: the two letters of gin and tonic

annotation.surface: An upmarket pub that serves both gin and tonics and proper food.
annotation.walkthrough: Fancy works twice: it stirs the letters, and it describes the smartened-up pub the whole clue defines. A gastropub is a British pub that serves restaurant-quality food.
annotation.definitionFit: A gastropub is a pub, a bar, that serves good food such as soup alongside drinks.

entries.clue: Sweet potatoes, peeled (3)

indicatorNotes.peeled: the word loses its outer letters, like skin

blocks.note: the outer S…S is stripped off

annotation.surface: Peeled sweet potatoes, the vegetable.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sweet potatoes" reads as the vegetable; the break is after Sweet, which is the British word for dessert. Pud is short for pudding.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain a sweet is a dessert, and pud is informal for pudding, a dessert.

entries.clue: Smashing lingerie worn by English monarch (8)

indicatorNotes.worn by: the lingerie is put on English, so wraps round the E

annotation.surface: A British king in stunning underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: Smashing sounds like British praise for the lingerie, but it means shattering. "Worn by" puts the underwear round the English.
annotation.definitionFit: Smashing and breaking both mean shattering something.

entries.clue: Tout withheld deposits, not all returned (6)

indicatorNotes.with: the answer is carried within the next words
indicatorNotes.not all: only part of the letters are used

annotation.surface: A tout keeps back people's deposits and doesn't hand them all back.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a ticket tout pocketing refunds. The letters run backwards across the gap between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To tout goods is to peddle them, pushing them on buyers.
